title: In Luke 11 How Can We Cultivate Perseverance In Our Prayer Life
paragraphs: Perseverance in Prayer: Lessons from Luke 11

Prayer is at the heart of the Christian life. In Luke 11, Jesus teaches His disciples not only how to pray, but also why to persist in prayer. This Bible study explores how we can cultivate perseverance in our prayer life, drawing directly from Jesus’ words and example.
The Model Prayer: Foundation for Perseverance
Luke 11 opens with the disciples asking Jesus to teach them to pray. Jesus responds by giving them what is commonly known as the Lord’s Prayer:

And he said unto them, When ye pray, say, Father, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Give us day by day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins; for we ourselves also forgive every one that is indebted to us. And bring us not into temptation. - Luke 11:2-4 ASV

This prayer is both a pattern and a reminder. It begins with God’s holiness and sovereignty, moves to our daily needs, and addresses forgiveness and spiritual protection. This structure keeps our prayers focused and persistent, not on our own desires, but on God’s will and our continual dependence on Him.
The Parable of the Persistent Friend
After teaching the Lord’s Prayer, Jesus tells a parable about persistence:

And he said unto them, Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go unto him at midnight, and say to him, Friend, lend me three loaves; ... though he will not rise and give him because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will arise and give him as many as he needeth. - Luke 11:5-8 ASV

The word "importunity" means shameless persistence or boldness. Jesus uses this story to illustrate that God welcomes our persistent prayers—not because He is reluctant or bothered, but because perseverance in prayer demonstrates faith and dependence on Him.
Jesus’ Promise: Ask, Seek, Knock
Jesus then gives us a direct encouragement to persevere in prayer:

And I say unto you, Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened. - Luke 11:9-10 ASV

Each verb—ask, seek, knock—implies ongoing action. Jesus is inviting us to come repeatedly and persistently to the Father. These are not empty rituals, but acts of faith in the God who hears and answers prayer.
God’s Character: The Motivation for Perseverance
Why can we persevere with confidence? Jesus assures us of the Father's goodness:
If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children, how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him? - Luke 11:13 ASV

God’s willingness to give—especially the gift of the Holy Spirit—far exceeds our expectations. This is the foundation for a persevering prayer life: we pray persistently, not to wear God down, but because He is a loving Father who delights to give us what we need most.
Practical Steps to Cultivate Perseverance in Prayer
Pray Regularly: Set aside specific times each day to pray, following the pattern Jesus gave.
Be Honest and Persistent: Bring your true needs and desires to God, even when answers are delayed.
Trust God’s Character: Remember that God is good and wise; He gives what is best, even if it isn’t always what we expect (Romans 8:28).
Pray with Others: The early church persisted in prayer together (Acts 1:14).
Conclusion

Perseverance in prayer is rooted in Christ’s teaching and example. As we persist, we grow in faith, deepen our relationship with God, and align our hearts with His will. Let us continue to ask, seek, and knock, confident that our Father hears and answers according to His perfect wisdom and love.
